name: Charles X of France

summary.text: Charles X was King of France from 1824 to 1830. On 17 April 1825 he issued an ordinance recognising the sovereignty of the former French part of Saint-Domingue (Haiti) in return for an indemnity of 150 million francs, payable in five annual instalments to the Caisse des Dépôts et Consignations, to compensate former colonists; the ordinance also reduced customs duties on French goods. Baron de Mackau delivered it with a naval squadron, and President Boyer accepted in July 1825. To meet the first instalment Haiti borrowed 30 million francs in Paris in November 1825 and received about 24 million after fees. In 1838 the indemnity was reduced to 90 million francs; the BnF records the indemnity paid off in 1878 and the 1825 and 1875 loans paid off in 1887–88 and 1921–22.

facts.claim: Charles X's ordinance of 17 April 1825 recognised Haiti's independence in exchange for 150 million francs, payable in five annual instalments, as compensation to former colonists.
facts.quote: France recognises the sovereignty of the former 'French part of Saint-Domingue' in return for compensation to be paid to the ex-property owning colonists.

sources.publisher: Bibliothèque nationale de France (France-Amériques heritage site)
sources.title: Haiti's independence debt. The slave as a unit of account (1794-1922)
When France extorted Haiti: the greatest heist in history

facts.claim: Baron de Mackau, sent by Charles X to deliver the ordinance, arrived in Haiti in July 1825 with a squadron of 14 warships; Haiti accepted the terms days later.
facts.quote: Baron de Mackau, whom Charles X sent to deliver the ordinance, arrived in Haiti in July, accompanied by a squadron of 14 brigs of war carrying more than 500 cannons.

sources.publisher: Canada Haiti Action Network (essay by Anthony Phillips)
sources.title: Haiti, France and the Independence Debt of 1825
How Haiti paid for its freedom

facts.claim: Haiti borrowed 30 million francs on the French market in November 1825; the loan was issued by the bankers Ternaux-Gandolphe et Cie at 80% of par with a 25-year maturity and 6% coupon, and Haiti received 24 million francs after bank commissions.
facts.quote: The loan was issued by the bankers Tenaux-Gandolphe et Cie, at 80% of par on the 4 November 1825. It had a maturity of 25 years and paid a yearly 6% coupon.

facts.claim: Haiti paid the first instalment of the indemnity but defaulted on the second in 1826, and serviced the 1825 loan in 1826 and 1827 only with help from the French Treasury.
facts.quote: Haiti managed to pay the first installment of the indemnity, only to default on the second installment the following year.

sources.title: A Debt of Dishonor (Oosterlinck, Panizza, Weidemaier, Gulati)

facts.claim: In 1838 France recognised Haiti's independence unconditionally and the indemnity was renegotiated to 90 million francs payable over 30 annual instalments; the 1825 loan's interest rate was reduced to 3% and repayment rescheduled.
facts.quote: In 1838, France recognised Haiti's independence, unconditionally this time. The total indemnity was renegotiated downwards (to 90 million francs), and its payment spread over 30 annual instalments.

facts.claim: The BnF heritage site states the independence debt was finally paid off in 1878 by way of a loan raised on the French market in 1875, and that the external loans of 1825 and 1875 were paid off in 1887–88 and 1921–22 respectively.
facts.quote: the external loans of 1825 and 1875 are, respectively, paid off in 1887-88 and in 1921-22.

connections.claim: According to Oosterlinck and co-authors, the banker Jacques Laffitte took over the obligations of Ternaux-Gandolphe et Cie on the 1825 Haitian loan in 1826; Laffitte claimed France had guaranteed the loan, while the French official Esmangart held in 1833 that France had guaranteed the indemnity but not the loan.
connections.quote: the banker Jacques Laffitte took over the obligations of Tenaux-Gandolphe et Cie in 1826

openQuestions: The site says a 'Laffitte-led consortium bought the bonds at 80% of face value'; the BU Law Review names Ternaux-Gandolphe et Cie as the issuer at 80% of par and places Laffitte's involvement from 1826. Which bankers formed the original underwriting syndicate should be checked in Oosterlinck et al. and Brière (2006).

The site says the last payments were made in 1947; the BnF puts the final payoff of the 1875 loan at 1921–22. The 1947 date (often tied to later National City Bank loans) was not supported by the sources consulted.
The site's '80% of Haitian revenue at points in the late 1800s' was not found in the sources consulted.

Sources differ on the 1838 figure: BnF and Brière give 90 million total; Oosterlinck et al. describe the remaining balance cut from 120 to 60 million. These are likely consistent (30 million already paid) but should be confirmed.
The Haitian payoff date is given as 1878 (BnF) and 1883 (Brière).
